steps.label: Definition

lines.text: Scutellum = the single, large, shield shaped

lines: It lies in a groove at one side of the
steps.why: The scutellum is simply the one cotyledon of a grass embryo given a special name; 'shield shaped' and 'at one side of the embryo axis' are the two identifying facts.
common_mistakes: Calling it a separate organ. It IS the cotyledon of the grass embryo.
Writing 'two cotyledons' — grasses are monocots; there is only one.
steps.memory_tip: Scutellum comes from the Latin word for shield — the name itself stores the shape.
steps.margin_note: The boxed definition with 'shield shaped cotyledon' is what earns this mark.

steps.label: Where it is found
lines: It is present in the endospermic seeds of
steps.why: The second half of the question asks the seed type: grass seeds keep their endosperm, so the scutellum sits against it and absorbs the food during germination.
common_mistakes: Answering 'monocot seeds' alone — say endospermic seeds of the grass family.
Giving bean or groundnut as the example; those are non-endospermic dicots.
steps.memory_tip: Maize grain: yellow endosperm + one shield-shaped scutellum pressed against it.
steps.margin_note: Name the seed type AND one example — the question asks both.

insider_note: Two asks, two marks: the definition and the seed type. Students who only define the scutellum leave the second mark on the table.
